title: Great Lines from the Classics
author: Various Classic Authors
description: Thirty short, unforgettable lines — one a day for thirty days — quoted straight from the twelve public-domain classics already in this Library (Austen, Dickens, Shelley, Carroll, Baum, Doyle, London, Stevenson, Burnett, Montgomery, Fitzgerald). A quick taste of each book's voice, for days when a whole chapter feels like too much.
source: Quoted verbatim from the public-domain full texts already bundled in this Library — see each line’s chapter credit.

chapters.title: Day 1
paragraphs: ‘And what is the use of a book,’ thought Alice ‘without pictures or conversations?’
— Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), opening line

chapters.title: Day 2
paragraphs: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
— Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813), opening line

chapters.title: Day 3
paragraphs: Marley was dead: to begin with. There is no doubt whatever about that.
— Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843), opening line

chapters.title: Day 4
paragraphs: There is no place like home.
— L. Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900)

chapters.title: Day 5
paragraphs: You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear.
— Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1892), “A Scandal in Bohemia”

chapters.title: Day 6
paragraphs: It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.
— Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818)

chapters.title: Day 7
paragraphs: Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!
— Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island (1883)

chapters.title: Day 8
paragraphs: If he be Mr. Hyde, I shall be Mr. Seek.
— Robert Louis Stevenson, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886)

chapters.title: Day 9
paragraphs: Isn’t it splendid to think of all the things there are to find out about?
— L. M. Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables (1908)

chapters.title: Day 10
paragraphs: Where you tend a rose, my lad, a thistle cannot grow.
— Frances Hodgson Burnett, The Secret Garden (1911)

chapters.title: Day 11
paragraphs: So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
— F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925), closing line

chapters.title: Day 12
paragraphs: He was sounding the deeps of his nature, and of the parts of his nature that were deeper than he, going back into the womb of Time.
— Jack London, The Call of the Wild (1903)

chapters.title: Day 13
paragraphs: Curiouser and curiouser!
— Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865)

chapters.title: Day 14
paragraphs: Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business.
— Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843)

chapters.title: Day 15
paragraphs: It is a capital mistake to theorize before one has data.
— Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1892), “A Scandal in Bohemia”

chapters.title: Day 16
paragraphs: I am malicious because I am miserable.
— Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818)

chapters.title: Day 17
paragraphs: Dead men don’t bite, you know.
— Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island (1883)

chapters.title: Day 18
paragraphs: Man is not truly one, but truly two.
— Robert Louis Stevenson, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886)

chapters.title: Day 19
paragraphs: Isn’t it nice to think that tomorrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?
— L. M. Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables (1908)

chapters.title: Day 20
paragraphs: Two things cannot be in one place.
— Frances Hodgson Burnett, The Secret Garden (1911)

chapters.title: Day 21
paragraphs: Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us.
— F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925)

chapters.title: Day 22
paragraphs: If I only had a heart, I should love them.
— L. Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900)

chapters.title: Day 23
paragraphs: We’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.
— Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865)

chapters.title: Day 24
paragraphs: When you have excluded the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth.
— Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1892), “The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet”

chapters.title: Day 25
paragraphs: I have described myself as always having been imbued with a fervent longing to penetrate the secrets of nature.
— Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818)

chapters.title: Day 26
paragraphs: I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year.
— Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843)

chapters.title: Day 27
paragraphs: A bosom friend—an intimate friend, you know—a really kindred spirit to whom I can confide my inmost soul.
— L. M. Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables (1908)

chapters.title: Day 28
paragraphs: Off with her head!
— Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), the Queen of Hearts

chapters.title: Day 29
paragraphs: “Can’t repeat the past?” he cried incredulously. “Why of course you can!”
— F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925)

chapters.title: Day 30
paragraphs: God bless us, every one!
— Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843), Tiny Tim
